Antibiotic Subscriptions Create a Second Commercialization Gate

The familiar case for antibiotic subscriptions starts with a market failure. A valuable new antibiotic should be used sparingly so that resistance develops slowly. That same stewardship principle suppresses sales, leaving developers unable to recover the cost of bringing narrow-spectrum or last-line drugs to market.

By Bottleneck Briefs · Published 2026-07-02 · 15 min read

In brief

  • £5m–£20m/year | England’s four maximum antimicrobial value bands
  • 2022 | England awarded its first two volume-delinked contracts
  • 59.1% | eligible US hospitals ever reporting one NHSN antimicrobial-use month
  • 35% | microbiology linkage in Scotland’s automated registry implementation
  • 2026–2028 | first scaled UK contracts will test operational readiness

Solving the revenue problem reveals the operating problem

England’s response was to pay for assessed value and availability rather than prescription volume. NICE and NHS England awarded the first subscription-style contracts in 2022 for ceftazidime-avibactam and cefiderocol. The suppliers receive quarterly payments that are not linked to the quantity dispensed. (NICE antimicrobial model)

That reform routes around the revenue gate. It does not complete commercialization.

Once the purchaser stops using sales volume as the main signal of value, the product has to function as an auditable access service. The supplier must keep it available. Hospitals must identify the right patients. Laboratories must produce credible susceptibility results. Stewardship teams must authorize restricted use. Registries and surveillance systems must capture what happened.

The emerging constraint is therefore sequential. A drug must first qualify clinically and win public funding. Only then do testing, supply, stewardship and evidence systems become material operating gates.

England is buying readiness, not doses

The expanded English model assigns qualifying products to one of four maximum annual value bands: £5 million, £10 million, £15 million or £20 million. A procurement notice published in August 2024 estimated the framework’s total potential value at £1.896 billion and planned for contracts to commence on April 1, 2026. (NHS England commercial guidance)

The £1.896 billion figure is a framework ceiling, not realized spending. By the July 23, 2026 forecast base date, the source record had not located an official product-level C299010 award notice identifying successful products or assigned bands. A June 2026 commission indicated that NICE was still completing final evaluations, suggesting that qualification and procurement were already running behind the original timetable.

The contract specification shows what the purchaser ultimately wants. Suppliers must maintain capacity equal to 30 months of anticipated demand, hold six months of physical stock in England, replenish that stock within 90 days, provide delivery within the specified 24-hour service window and achieve at least 95% on-time-in-full performance. The contract also covers stewardship, resistance monitoring, surveillance support and environmental manufacturing practice. (NHS contract annex)

This resembles a long-dated preparedness contract more than a pharmaceutical royalty. The manufacturer receives predictable revenue, but it also finances idle capacity, inventory, expiry risk, compliance and rapid delivery for a product that may rarely be used.

The commercial skill set changes accordingly. Broad promotion matters less. Tender evidence, health-technology assessment, contract compliance, inventory management and purchaser relations matter more.

The hospital has to reconstruct a rare clinical event

The clinical pathway begins before the antibiotic reaches the pharmacy:

resistant-infection suspicion → specimen → organism or resistance identification → susceptibility interpretation → specialist authorization → dispensing → administration → outcome → surveillance

No single institution or software supplier controls that chain.

NICE restricts the two pilot drugs to severe resistant Gram-negative infections when suitable alternatives are unavailable. Decisions should draw on specialist microbiology advice, susceptibility testing and evidence about the resistance mechanism. (NICE AMR1 recommendations)

NICE also recommends collecting infection site, specimen type, pathogen, resistance mechanism, treatment duration, mortality, clinical cure, microbiological eradication, adverse events and hospital-resource use. These fields sit across laboratory information systems, electronic health records, pharmacy systems, ward records and registries.

High-volume medicines produce abundant records as a side effect of routine use. Reserved antibiotics generate small cohorts in which every missing result matters. Hospitals must deliberately link the records around each case.

The UK Antimicrobial Registry reports more than 1,100 patients across 60 sites. Its published hospital-registry cohort was smaller, and researchers identified prospective recruitment, manual data entry, staff capacity and inconsistent local systems as limits on completeness. (UKAR)

Scotland’s UKAR Virtual Registry shows the relief path. It uses linked electronic health records rather than relying entirely on prospective manual abstraction. The reported implementation identified 308 patients and 353 prescriptions. Yet microbiology results could be linked for only about 35% of patients.

Automation reduced one form of work while exposing another: shared identifiers, standardized fields and reliable linkage were still incomplete. The bottleneck moved from typing records into connecting them correctly.

Cefiderocol shows how a laboratory detail becomes a market gate

Cefiderocol illustrates the diagnostic layer because its susceptibility testing is unusually demanding.

CLSI reported in 2023 that broth microdilution required iron-depleted, cation-adjusted Mueller-Hinton broth and that cefiderocol was not then available on automated antimicrobial-susceptibility systems. Breakpoint differences between CLSI, the FDA and EUCAST added interpretive complexity. (CLSI cefiderocol update)

The claim needs a date. Cefiderocol testing itself was not unavailable. The FDA had cleared a manual MIC route in 2020, followed by disc-diffusion and other manual routes. The unresolved question in 2026 was whether standardized automated support had become widely available across hospital platforms.

A 2025 Journal of Clinical Microbiology study found that broth source and preparation affected MIC reproducibility. After six hours of chelation, agreement within one dilution reached 96.5% for BD-BBL versus BD-Difco media, compared with 62.4% for BD-BBL versus Merck and 58.8% for BD-Difco versus Merck. (JCM media study)

Those differences concern a laboratory consumable, but they can influence whether a clinician classifies an organism as susceptible and whether a last-line drug is used. Qualified media, current breakpoints, validation isolates and device clearance therefore sit inside the commercialization pathway.

This does not mean every reserved antibiotic will create the same diagnostic constraint. Cefiderocol may be an unusually difficult case. The relevant question is product-specific: how long does it take after approval or subscription award for routine hospital systems to support a reliable test?

The United States has a reporting substrate, not a subscription market

The proposed US PASTEUR Act makes the same operating architecture explicit. H.R.7352, introduced on February 4, 2026, proposed annual contracts of $75 million to $300 million per product. It also included commercial availability, reliable supply, stewardship, resistance reporting, post-market studies, manufacturing practices and provision of antimicrobial material to susceptibility-test manufacturers. (H.R.7352 introduced text)

It remained proposed legislation at the forecast base date. The United States should therefore not be described as operating a federal antibiotic-subscription program.

The CDC’s National Healthcare Safety Network nevertheless provides part of the infrastructure such a program could use. As of January 1, 2025, 4,362 hospitals—59.1% of eligible hospitals—had submitted at least one month of antimicrobial-use data. The 2024 adult analytical dataset contained 3,288 hospitals with at least nine months of data across 18,824 eligible locations. (CDC 2024 AU report)

“Ever submitted one month” is a low readiness threshold. It does not demonstrate continuous reporting, reliable resistance data or linkage between a particular drug, organism and patient outcome.

CDC also reported that 97% of US hospitals met its seven basic stewardship Core Elements in 2024. Only 16% met all six more advanced priorities, while 36% met five. The distinction matters: a hospital can have a formal stewardship program without possessing complete, validated, product-level data infrastructure.

US surveillance is consequently broad but uneven. CMS requirements are expanding electronic reporting, yet hospitals can still face exclusions or implementation barriers when they lack compatible medication-administration, admission-discharge-transfer or laboratory feeds.

The cases do not support a single universal bottleneck. They show a sequence. Sweden first needed suppliers to launch and hold stock. England’s scaled model first has to complete product evaluation and contracting. Hospitals then have to execute the access, testing and evidence obligations. The proposed US model must still clear Congress before those downstream questions become commercially relevant.

Sweden demonstrates that a simpler contract can work

Sweden’s pilot is the strongest counterexample to the claim that sophisticated patient-level evidence must come first.

From July 2020 through December 2022, the Public Health Agency of Sweden used minimum annual revenue guarantees to improve the availability of selected antibiotics in a small, restrictive market. Participating companies combined guaranteed income with stock and delivery obligations. The agency reported that several important products became available earlier than in comparable European markets. (Swedish Public Health Agency)

Sweden did not first build the full English architecture of product-value bands and extensive patient-level outcomes linkage. It targeted the narrower availability problem.

The agency still called for recurring assessment of medical need and surveillance of responsible use. Once a supplier is paid to maintain a product that seldom sells, the public purchaser must monitor whether the contract remains necessary and whether unused inventory is being managed sensibly.

The lesson is not that evidence is irrelevant. It is that contract design determines which evidence is required and when. A simple availability guarantee can improve access before a comprehensive value-measurement system exists.

Value can migrate without creating a large new vendor market

The clearest direct beneficiary of a subscription contract is the qualified antimicrobial sponsor. Revenue becomes less sensitive to prescription volume and more dependent on product eligibility, value-band assignment, contract duration and renewal.

Risk does not disappear. It changes form. The sponsor trades demand risk for qualification, policy, supply, compliance and renewal risk. Public purchasers gain leverage because they control entry into the subscription category and can leave nonqualifying products on conventional reimbursement.

Several complementary capabilities could attract spending:

  • AST instruments, panels, discs, media and validation materials;
  • reference-laboratory testing for hospitals without local methods;
  • LIS, EHR and pharmacy interfaces;
  • antimicrobial registries and data-quality services;
  • stewardship staffing and decision support;
  • safety stock, warehousing and rapid distribution;
  • environmental verification and manufacturing compliance.

Technical necessity does not guarantee attractive margins. Reserved drugs generate low test volumes by design. Hospital integration can be customized and labor-intensive. Registry support may be funded inside the sponsor’s annual contract rather than purchased as a separate service.

The broad diagnostics platforms now housed in Waters Advanced Diagnostics—including businesses combined with Waters from BD in February 2026—have relevant microbiology instruments, consumables and services. Their large installed bases may help them support new antimicrobial workflows. But Waters’ total diagnostics revenue cannot be counted as evidence of subscription-driven demand; no attributable order or material revenue pool was identified.

The same caution applies to hospital-software vendors. CMS reporting requirements already create demand for antimicrobial-use and resistance interfaces independently of subscription policy. Counting all related interoperability expenditure as a new antibiotic-subscription market would double-count an existing compliance transition.

The historical base rate keeps the drug pipeline in the foreground

Achaogen is the closest warning about what subscription policy is trying to fix. The company launched plazomicin into a narrow resistant-infection market, recorded about $0.8 million in 2018 sales and faced an estimated annual cash burn of roughly $60 million. It filed for bankruptcy in 2019.

That episode shows why conventional unit economics fail even after regulatory approval. A developer can produce a clinically useful antibiotic, conserve it correctly and still become insolvent because appropriate use produces inadequate revenue.

Today’s subscription models directly address that post-approval cash-flow drought. The difference is that England also packages payment with supply, stewardship, environmental and surveillance obligations. The closest precedent solved neither the developer’s economics nor the full operating stack; current policy is attempting both.

Yet the pipeline may still bind first. If too few products offer sufficient novelty or clinical value, sophisticated registries and automated AST systems will sit underused. England’s delayed scaled procurement may ultimately reveal a shortage of qualifying products rather than a failure of hospital data infrastructure.

The narrower thesis is therefore stronger: evidence and operability become important after a product clears the earlier gates. They are not yet proven to be the dominant constraint across the market.

Who controls the second gate

NICE and NHS England control product qualification, value-band assignment and contract design. Sponsors control the medicine, manufacturing arrangements and much of the safety stock. Hospitals control whether clinical cases are recognized, tested and documented. Stewardship teams control authorization in practice.

FDA, CLSI and EUCAST influence whether susceptibility results can be generated and interpreted using accepted methods. AST manufacturers decide when a new drug reaches installed automated platforms. EHR, LIS and pharmacy vendors control interfaces that may require costly local validation. UKAR, UKHSA and CDC/NHSN control important aggregation and surveillance routes.

Control is fragmented, which makes relief difficult. Paying the sponsor does not compel a hospital to replace its laboratory system, resolve identifier mismatches or fund additional stewardship staff. A public contract can establish obligations, but execution still depends on organizations outside the developer’s direct authority.

This fragmentation also limits vendor capture. A supplier can own one critical node without controlling the whole workflow. Durable leverage will belong to the actors whose output becomes necessary for qualification, routine use or renewal—and whose work cannot be substituted easily.

What would prove the thesis wrong

The thesis would weaken materially if England awards and renews several subscription contracts while product-level registry completeness, integrated hospital feeds and automated AST support remain limited and do not affect payment or renewal.

It would also weaken if procurement records show that delays come almost entirely from a thin product pipeline, inadequate clinical differentiation or public-budget constraints. In that case, evidence infrastructure would be a downstream implementation detail rather than a central commercialization gate.

A third falsifier would be rapid technical relief before the market scales: broad EHR-linked registry deployment, high microbiology completeness, near-universal NHSN reporting and timely automated AST panels for each new product.

The strongest alternative is Sweden’s. If more countries improve access through simple minimum-revenue and stock guarantees without adopting extensive product-level evidence requirements, the English design will look like one institutional choice rather than the inevitable endpoint of delinked payment.

What to watch

  • December 31, 2026: an official C299010 notice names at least one successful product and supplier.
  • 2027: England publishes assigned value bands, scoring rationales or executed product schedules.
  • December 31, 2027: FDA clears an automated cefiderocol susceptibility-testing indication.
  • March 31, 2028: a UK document reports stock, OTIF, stewardship or data-quality performance.
  • March 31, 2030: at least two non-pilot products have received UK subscription contracts.

Antibiotic subscriptions can solve a genuine financing failure, but they do not turn a reserved drug into a functioning public-health asset by themselves. After payment comes qualification; after qualification comes testing, stock, stewardship and evidence. The first scaled English contracts will show whether that second gate is a manageable compliance layer or the next industrial bottleneck.
